export default "---\ntitle: 'Multi-Head Attention: Why One Subspace Was Never Enough'\ndate: '2024-10-30'\nslug: 'multi-head-attention'\ntags: ['Deep Learning', 'Transformers', 'Attention', 'NLP']\ncategory: ['ML & Deep Learning', 'Transformers']\nexcerpt: 'A single attention head can only compute one weighted mixture per token — multi-head attention runs h independent heads in parallel and concatenates.'\nstatus: 'draft'\n---\n\n![Multi-head attention architecture: input X fans out to h=2 independent projection heads, each computes scaled dot-product attention, outputs are concatenated and projected through W^O back to d_model](../Assets/blogs/multi-head-attention-overview.png)\n_A single input splits into h parallel branches. Each branch runs its own learned Q/K/V projections and attention function, yielding a d_v-dimensional output. Those outputs are concatenated and projected back to d_model through W^O — with no extra compute cost over a single wide head._\n\n## Where the Last Post Left Off\n\nIf you haven't read [Self-Attention from First Principles](https://ankitkr8540.github.io/portfolio/#/blogs/self-attention-from-first-principles), start there. This post picks up from its final observation: self-attention handles context mixing, but \"multiple heads handle representational diversity.\" That sentence was deliberately left unexplained. The question it defers is the exact question this post answers.\n\nTo recap what was derived: for the sequence \"trophy was big,\" the \"big\" token computes a query vector $\\mathbf{q}_{\\text{big}} = [1, 1]$, takes dot products against every key, scales, and applies softmax to get attention weights $\\alpha = [0.575, 0.140, 0.285]$. \"Big\" attends to \"trophy\" at weight 0.575 — the size adjective correctly finds the noun it modifies. One pass, no recurrence, no bottleneck.\n\nThat looks like it's working. So what's the problem?\n\n## The Single-Head Ceiling\n\nThe same sentence contains more than one relationship. \"Big\" needs to find \"trophy\" — that's semantic. \"Was\" needs to find \"trophy\" as its subject — that's syntactic. In a real parsing task, \"was\" might also need to find \"big\" as its predicate complement. These are distinct relationships, and they require the model to simultaneously track different types of alignment across the same four tokens.\n\nA single attention head computes one attention distribution per token per layer. \"Big\" gets one set of weights over all other tokens — it cannot simultaneously attend to \"trophy\" for one purpose and to \"was\" for another. The weights must average over all the relationships the model needs to express, and averaging is lossy. You cannot recover \"I want 75% on semantic grounds and 25% on syntactic grounds\" from a single softmax distribution that tries to serve both needs at once.\n\nVaswani et al. put it plainly in section 3.2 of \"Attention Is All You Need\": \"With a single attention head, averaging inhibits [jointly attending to information from different representation subspaces at different positions].\" That sentence is worth unpacking. The word \"averaging\" is doing real work. When a single head produces its output vector for a token, it computes a weighted mixture of all value vectors. One set of weights, one mixture. If the model needs to simultaneously ask \"which token am I semantically related to?\" and \"which token am I syntactically linked to?\", a single set of softmax weights cannot answer both questions separately. The answers get blended — and blending loses the distinction between them.\n\nThe fix is to not blend. Run multiple independent attention functions on the same input, each operating in its own lower-dimensional subspace, and concatenate their outputs.\n\n## Independent Subspaces: What They Are and Why the Cost Stays the Same\n\nThe model dimension $d_{\\text{model}}$ is the length of each token's embedding vector. In the base Transformer, $d_{\\text{model}} = 512$. A single attention head would project each token's embedding to query, key, and value vectors of dimension $d_k = d_v = 512$ — working in the full embedding space.\n\nMulti-head attention instead splits: if you use $h = 8$ heads, each head gets $d_k = d_v = d_{\\text{model}} / h = 64$ dimensions to work in. Each head has its own independent projection matrices $W_Q^i, W_K^i, W_V^i$ — none of the weights are shared across heads. Head 1 learns one subspace; head 2 learns another; they have no obligation to agree, and in practice they don't.\n\nThe key observation about cost: one head with $d_k = 512$ and eight heads each with $d_k = 64$ require the same number of floating-point operations. In the first case, you do one large dot product. In the second, you do eight smaller ones. The matrix multiply cost per head scales with $d_k$, so eight heads at $64$ dimensions each is computationally equivalent to one head at $512$ dimensions — as the paper notes: \"Due to the reduced dimension of each head, the total computational cost is similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality.\"\n\nThis matters because it means multi-head attention costs nothing extra. You trade one large undifferentiated attention distribution for several small specialized ones, for free.\n\n## Worked Example: Two Heads on \"Trophy Was Big\"\n\nThe same setup as the [self-attention post](/blog/self-attention-from-first-principles): three tokens, 4-dimensional embeddings, $h = 2$ heads, $d_k = d_v = 2$.\n\n| dim | meaning        |\n| --- | -------------- |\n| 0   | noun-like      |\n| 1   | verb-like      |\n| 2   | adjective-like |\n| 3   | size-related   |\n\nToken embeddings:\n\n$$\\mathbf{x}_{\\text{trophy}} = [1, 0, 0, 1], \\quad \\mathbf{x}_{\\text{was}} = [0, 1, 0, 0], \\quad \\mathbf{x}_{\\text{big}} = [0, 0, 1, 1]$$\n\n### Head 1: The Semantic Head\n\nHead 1's projection matrices are identical to those derived in the self-attention post — they're designed to extract adjective-ness and size-relatedness on the query side (to ask \"what is this describing?\") and noun-ness and size-capability on the key side (to answer \"what can be described by size?\"):\n\n$$W_Q^1 = \\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\\\0&0\\\\1&0\\\\0&1\\end{bmatrix}, \\quad W_K^1 = \\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\\\0&0\\\\0&0\\\\0&1\\end{bmatrix}, \\quad W_V^1 = \\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\\\0&1\\\\0&0\\\\0&0\\end{bmatrix}$$\n\n**Step 1 (Head 1) — Compute queries and keys.**\n\n$$\\mathbf{q}^1_{\\text{trophy}} = [0,\\; 1], \\quad \\mathbf{q}^1_{\\text{was}} = [0,\\; 0], \\quad \\mathbf{q}^1_{\\text{big}} = [1,\\; 1]$$\n\n$$\\mathbf{k}^1_{\\text{trophy}} = [1,\\; 1], \\quad \\mathbf{k}^1_{\\text{was}} = [0,\\; 0], \\quad \\mathbf{k}^1_{\\text{big}} = [0,\\; 1]$$\n\n**Step 2 (Head 1) — Attention scores for \"big\" as the query.**\n\n$$e_{\\text{big} \\to \\text{trophy}}^1 = [1,1] \\cdot [1,1] = 2, \\quad e_{\\text{big} \\to \\text{was}}^1 = 0, \\quad e_{\\text{big} \\to \\text{big}}^1 = 1$$\n\nAfter scaling by $\\sqrt{2}$ and softmax:\n\n$$\\alpha^1_{\\text{big}} = [0.575,\\;\\; 0.140,\\;\\; 0.285]$$\n\n**Step 3 (Head 1) — Values and output for \"big\".**\n\n$$\\mathbf{v}^1_{\\text{trophy}} = [1,\\; 0], \\quad \\mathbf{v}^1_{\\text{was}} = [0,\\; 1], \\quad \\mathbf{v}^1_{\\text{big}} = [0,\\; 0]$$\n\n$$\\mathbf{o}^1_{\\text{big}} = 0.575 \\cdot [1,0] + 0.140 \\cdot [0,1] + 0.285 \\cdot [0,0] = [0.575,\\;\\; 0.140]$$\n\nHead 1's output for \"big\" carries a strong noun-entity signal (0.575 from \"trophy\") and a faint verb signal (0.140 from \"was\"). This is the semantic relationship: size-adjective finds its noun.\n\n### Head 2: The Syntactic Head\n\nHead 2's projection matrices are designed around a different question. On the query side, they extract verb-ness (dim 1) and noun-ness (dim 0) — asking \"what syntactic role am I playing?\" On the key side, they extract noun-ness (dim 0) and adjective-ness (dim 2) — answering \"what syntactic constituents can I link to?\"\n\n$$W_Q^2 = \\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\\\1&0\\\\0&0\\\\0&0\\end{bmatrix}, \\quad W_K^2 = \\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\\\0&0\\\\0&1\\\\0&0\\end{bmatrix}, \\quad W_V^2 = \\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\\\1&0\\\\0&0\\\\0&0\\end{bmatrix}$$\n\n**Step 1 (Head 2) — Compute queries and keys.**\n\n$$\\mathbf{q}^2_{\\text{trophy}} = [0,\\; 1], \\quad \\mathbf{q}^2_{\\text{was}} = [1,\\; 0], \\quad \\mathbf{q}^2_{\\text{big}} = [0,\\; 0]$$\n\n$$\\mathbf{k}^2_{\\text{trophy}} = [1,\\; 0], \\quad \\mathbf{k}^2_{\\text{was}} = [0,\\; 0], \\quad \\mathbf{k}^2_{\\text{big}} = [0,\\; 1]$$\n\n**Step 2 (Head 2) — Attention scores.**\n\nFor \"was\" as query ($\\mathbf{q}^2_{\\text{was}} = [1, 0]$):\n\n$$e_{\\text{was} \\to \\text{trophy}}^2 = [1,0] \\cdot [1,0] = 1, \\quad e_{\\text{was} \\to \\text{was}}^2 = 0, \\quad e_{\\text{was} \\to \\text{big}}^2 = 0$$\n\nScaling by $\\sqrt{2}$ gives $[0.707, 0, 0]$. Softmax: $e^{0.707} \\approx 2.028$; sum $= 4.028$.\n\n$$\\alpha^2_{\\text{was}} = [0.504,\\;\\; 0.248,\\;\\; 0.248]$$\n\nThe verb \"was\" attends to \"trophy\" at 0.504 in head 2 — the copula finds its subject.\n\nFor \"trophy\" as query ($\\mathbf{q}^2_{\\text{trophy}} = [0, 1]$):\n\n$$e_{\\text{trophy} \\to \\text{trophy}}^2 = 0, \\quad e_{\\text{trophy} \\to \\text{was}}^2 = 0, \\quad e_{\\text{trophy} \\to \\text{big}}^2 = [0,1] \\cdot [0,1] = 1$$\n\nScaling gives $[0, 0, 0.707]$. Softmax: sum $= 4.028$.\n\n$$\\alpha^2_{\\text{trophy}} = [0.248,\\;\\; 0.248,\\;\\; 0.504]$$\n\n\"Trophy\" attends to \"big\" at 0.504 — the subject finds its predicative adjective.\n\nFor \"big\" as query ($\\mathbf{q}^2_{\\text{big}} = [0, 0]$): all dot products are zero, softmax gives uniform weights $[0.333, 0.333, 0.333]$. \"Big\" has no syntactic signal to exploit in head 2's subspace.\n\n**Step 3 (Head 2) — Values and outputs.**\n\n$$\\mathbf{v}^2_{\\text{trophy}} = [0,\\; 1], \\quad \\mathbf{v}^2_{\\text{was}} = [1,\\; 0], \\quad \\mathbf{v}^2_{\\text{big}} = [0,\\; 0]$$\n\n$$\\mathbf{o}^2_{\\text{big}} = 0.333 \\cdot [0,1] + 0.333 \\cdot [1,0] + 0.333 \\cdot [0,0] = [0.333,\\;\\; 0.333]$$\n\n$$\\mathbf{o}^2_{\\text{was}} = 0.504 \\cdot [0,1] + 0.248 \\cdot [1,0] + 0.248 \\cdot [0,0] = [0.248,\\;\\; 0.504]$$\n\n### Concatenation and the Output Projection\n\nEach head produces a $d_v = 2$ dimensional output vector per token. With $h = 2$ heads, each token now has two 2-dimensional vectors — one from each head. These are concatenated into a single 4-dimensional vector:\n\n$$\\text{concat}(\\mathbf{o}^1_{\\text{big}},\\; \\mathbf{o}^2_{\\text{big}}) = [0.575,\\;\\; 0.140,\\;\\; 0.333,\\;\\; 0.333]$$\n\n$$\\text{concat}(\\mathbf{o}^1_{\\text{was}},\\; \\mathbf{o}^2_{\\text{was}}) = [0.333,\\;\\; 0.333,\\;\\; 0.248,\\;\\; 0.504]$$\n\nThe concatenated vector has dimension $h \\cdot d_v = 4 = d_{\\text{model}}$. A final learned projection matrix $W^O \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_{\\text{model}} \\times d_{\\text{model}}}$ maps this back to $d_{\\text{model}}$-dimensional space — blending the information from both heads into a single output representation. In this toy example, using $W^O = I_4$ (identity) to keep the arithmetic transparent, the final output for each token is:\n\n$$\\mathbf{o}_{\\text{big}} = [0.575,\\;\\; 0.140,\\;\\; 0.333,\\;\\; 0.333]$$\n\n$$\\mathbf{o}_{\\text{was}} = [0.333,\\;\\; 0.333,\\;\\; 0.248,\\;\\; 0.504]$$\n\n### What the Output Now Carries\n\nLook at what these representations contain. \"Big\" entered the multi-head attention block with zero noun information ($x_{\\text{big}} = [0, 0, 1, 1]$, noun dim is 0). Its output now has 0.575 in the noun-entity slot, borrowed from \"trophy\" via head 1's semantic alignment. Its head-2 slots are balanced at 0.333 — \"big\" had no syntactic signal to exploit in that subspace, so it gets nothing useful there, and that's correct.\n\n\"Was\" tells the more interesting story. Head 1 gave it a uniform distribution (its query vector in head 1's subspace was $[0, 0]$ — no signal). Head 2 gave it $[0.248, 0.504]$: the verb's output now carries significant noun-entity information borrowed from \"trophy\" through the copula→subject relationship. A single head could not have done both things simultaneously for both \"big\" and \"was\" using one set of projection weights.\n\n![Head 1 and Head 2 attention weight matrices for \"trophy was big\" — showing complementary, non-overlapping relationship patterns](../Assets/blogs/multi-head-attention-heads.png)\n_Head 1 (left): \"big\" attends to \"trophy\" at 0.575 — the adjective finds its noun. Head 2 (right): \"was\" attends to \"trophy\" at 0.504 and \"trophy\" attends to \"big\" at 0.504 — the copula links subject and predicate. Neither pattern appears in the other head. One head could not have captured both._\n\nIn general: each head learns to specialize in a particular type of alignment. The concatenated output carries the results of all those alignments independently, without any head having to compromise its weights to serve a competing relationship type.\n\n## The General Formula\n\n$$\\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \\text{Concat}(\\text{head}_1, \\ldots, \\text{head}_h)\\, W^O$$\n\nwhere each head is:\n\n$$\\text{head}_i = \\text{Attention}(Q W_Q^i,\\;\\; K W_K^i,\\;\\; V W_V^i) = \\text{softmax}\\!\\left(\\frac{(Q W_Q^i)(K W_K^i)^\\top}{\\sqrt{d_k}}\\right)(V W_V^i)$$\n\nThe projection matrices have shapes:\n\n$$W_Q^i \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_{\\text{model}} \\times d_k}, \\quad W_K^i \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_{\\text{model}} \\times d_k}, \\quad W_V^i \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_{\\text{model}} \\times d_v}, \\quad W^O \\in \\mathbb{R}^{h d_v \\times d_{\\text{model}}}$$\n\nEvery matrix in this formula is learned. The model is not told which head should specialize in syntax and which in semantics — it discovers whatever specializations are useful for the task, through backpropagation. In practice, different heads do emerge with different behavior (positional heads that attend to neighboring tokens, semantic heads that track topical similarity, coreference heads), but this is emergent, not designed.\n\n## What the Empirical Evidence Shows\n\nVaswani et al. report a head-count ablation in Table 3 of [\"Attention Is All You Need\"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762), holding all other hyperparameters constant and varying only $h$, adjusting $d_k$ proportionally to keep total compute fixed:\n\n| Heads ($h$) |  $d_k$ | BLEU (EN→DE dev) |\n| ----------: | -----: | ---------------: |\n|           1 |    512 |             24.9 |\n|           4 |    128 |             25.5 |\n|       **8** | **64** |         **25.8** |\n|          16 |     32 |             25.4 |\n|          32 |     16 |             25.1 |\n\nA single head ($h = 1$) with $d_k = 512$ — a single attention function with full dimensionality — scores 24.9 BLEU. The 8-head model scores 25.8 BLEU. That's a 0.9-point gap for a mechanism that costs the same compute. The paper notes: \"single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting.\"\n\nThe degradation at $h = 16$ and $h = 32$ matters too. More heads means each head operates in an increasingly narrow subspace — 16 dimensions per head at $h = 32$. At that scale, there isn't enough capacity per head to learn a useful alignment pattern, and performance falls off. The sweet spot is $h = 8$ with $d_k = 64$. These values were chosen by ablation, not by theory, and they're not universal — larger models often use more heads (GPT-3's 96-head attention operates at $d_{\\text{model}} = 12288$, $d_k = 128$ per head).\n\nThe takeaway is narrow but important: the gain from multiple heads is real and measurable, it's not proportional to the number of heads, and it comes at no computational premium.\n\n## Code: Multi-Head Attention from Scratch\n\n```python\nimport numpy as np\n\ndef softmax(x, axis=-1):\n    \"\"\"Numerically stable softmax.\"\"\"\n    x = x - np.max(x, axis=axis, keepdims=True)\n    e = np.exp(x)\n    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)\n\ndef single_head_attention(Q, K, V):\n    \"\"\"Scaled dot-product attention for one head.\"\"\"\n    d_k = Q.shape[-1]\n    scores = (Q @ K.T) / np.sqrt(d_k)   # (n, n)\n    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)   # row-wise softmax\n    return weights @ V, weights          # (n, d_v), (n, n)\n\ndef multi_head_attention(X, Wqs, Wks, Wvs, Wo):\n    \"\"\"\n    Multi-head self-attention.\n\n    Args:\n        X:   (n, d_model)  token embeddings\n        Wqs: list of h matrices, each (d_model, d_k)\n        Wks: list of h matrices, each (d_model, d_k)\n        Wvs: list of h matrices, each (d_model, d_v)\n        Wo:  (h*d_v, d_model)  output projection\n\n    Returns:\n        output:  (n, d_model)\n        weights: list of h attention matrices, each (n, n)\n    \"\"\"\n    head_outputs = []\n    all_weights  = []\n\n    for Wq, Wk, Wv in zip(Wqs, Wks, Wvs):\n        Q = X @ Wq   # (n, d_k)\n        K = X @ Wk\n        V = X @ Wv   # (n, d_v)\n        out, w = single_head_attention(Q, K, V)\n        head_outputs.append(out)   # (n, d_v)\n        all_weights.append(w)\n\n    # Concatenate along the feature axis: (n, h*d_v)\n    concat = np.concatenate(head_outputs, axis=-1)\n\n    # Project back to d_model\n    output = concat @ Wo   # (n, d_model)\n    return output, all_weights\n\n\n# ── Reproduce the worked example ──────────────────────────────────────────────\nX = np.array([\n    [1, 0, 0, 1],   # \"trophy\": noun, size-capable\n    [0, 1, 0, 0],   # \"was\":    verb\n    [0, 0, 1, 1],   # \"big\":    adjective, size-related\n], dtype=float)\n\n# Head 1 — semantic subspace (adjective-size → noun-size)\nWq1 = np.array([[0,0],[0,0],[1,0],[0,1]], dtype=float)\nWk1 = np.array([[1,0],[0,0],[0,0],[0,1]], dtype=float)\nWv1 = np.array([[1,0],[0,1],[0,0],[0,0]], dtype=float)\n\n# Head 2 — syntactic subspace (verb/noun → argument linking)\nWq2 = np.array([[0,1],[1,0],[0,0],[0,0]], dtype=float)\nWk2 = np.array([[1,0],[0,0],[0,1],[0,0]], dtype=float)\nWv2 = np.array([[0,1],[1,0],[0,0],[0,0]], dtype=float)\n\n# Output projection: identity for transparency\nWo = np.eye(4)\n\noutput, weights = multi_head_attention(X, [Wq1, Wq2], [Wk1, Wk2], [Wv1, Wv2], Wo)\n\ntokens = [\"trophy\", \"was\", \"big\"]\nfor h_idx, w in enumerate(weights):\n    label = [\"Semantic (Head 1)\", \"Syntactic (Head 2)\"][h_idx]\n    print(f\"\\n{label} attention weights:\")\n    print(f\"{'':>8}\", \" \".join(f\"{t:>8}\" for t in tokens))\n    for i, row in enumerate(w):\n        print(f\"{tokens[i]:>8}\", \" \".join(f\"{v:>8.3f}\" for v in row))\n\nprint(\"\\nFinal multi-head outputs:\")\nfor i, (tok, o) in enumerate(zip(tokens, output)):\n    print(f\"  {tok}: {np.round(o, 3)}\")\n```\n\nRunning this reproduces the exact values from the worked example. The attention weight matrix for head 1 shows \"big\" attending to \"trophy\" at 0.575; head 2 shows \"was\" attending to \"trophy\" at 0.504 and \"trophy\" attending to \"big\" at 0.504. No single head could have produced both patterns simultaneously.\n\n## Where Multi-Head Attention Lives in the Transformer\n\nThe Transformer uses multi-head attention in three distinct roles, and distinguishing them matters:\n\n**Encoder self-attention** — Each encoder layer runs multi-head self-attention over the input sequence. Every token attends to every other input token. There are no causal restrictions. This is where the encoder builds its contextual representations of the source.\n\n**Decoder self-attention** — The decoder also runs self-attention, but with a causal mask: token at position $i$ can only attend to positions $\\leq i$. This ensures that during training, the decoder cannot cheat by looking at future target tokens. The masking is implemented by setting future positions to $-\\infty$ before softmax, which makes their weights zero.\n\n**Encoder-decoder cross-attention** — Each decoder layer also has a cross-attention sub-layer in which the queries come from the decoder's current state and the keys and values come from the encoder's output. This is how the decoder learns to pull specific source information when generating each target token. The encoder runs once; its output is reused as $K$ and $V$ in every decoder layer.\n\nMulti-head attention handles all three roles with the same formula — only the source of $Q$, $K$, $V$ changes. This uniformity is part of what makes the Transformer's architecture surprisingly modular.\n\n## What Multi-Head Attention Still Cannot Do\n\n**Position is still invisible.** Like single-head attention, multi-head attention is permutation-invariant. Feeding the tokens in reverse order produces different per-token outputs (because query-key pairings shift) but the operation itself has no representation of token order. Positional encodings added to the input embeddings are what give the model access to sequence order — without them, the model cannot tell \"The cat sat on the mat\" from \"The mat sat on the cat.\"\n\n**Specialization is not guaranteed.** The fact that heads can specialize does not mean they will specialize usefully. In practice, many heads learn near-identical patterns, and [Michel et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10650) showed that in BERT and machine translation models, a significant fraction of heads can be pruned at test time with minimal performance loss. The model learns to hedge, distributing information redundantly across heads rather than assigning each head a clean role. This is an optimization landscape problem, not a design flaw that multi-head attention could resolve by construction.\n\n**The quadratic cost remains.** Each head still computes an $n \\times n$ score matrix. With $h$ heads each at $d_k = d_{\\text{model}}/h$, the total attention computation is $O(n^2 d_{\\text{model}})$ — the same asymptotic cost as single-head attention. Multi-head attention's efficiency argument is that it achieves better quality for the same compute, not that it reduces the compute for a given sequence length. Long-context architectures (FlashAttention, Mamba, linear attention) address the quadratic cost separately.\n\n**Learned subspaces are opaque.** You cannot look at head 3 of a trained Transformer and read off what it's specialized in. Mechanistic interpretability work ([Elhage et al. 2021, \"A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits\"](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html)) has made real progress at reverse-engineering what heads do, but this is non-trivial research, not a natural consequence of the architecture. Multi-head attention gives the model the _capacity_ to specialize; whether and how it does is learned from data.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Attention Is All You Need — Vaswani et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)\n- [Are Sixteen Heads Really Better Than One? — Michel et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10650)\n- [A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits — Elhage et al. (2021)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html)\n";
