export default "---\ntitle: 'Layer Normalization: Why Batch Statistics Break for Sequences'\ndate: '2024-11-5'\nslug: 'layer-normalization'\ntags: ['Deep Learning', 'Transformers', 'Normalization', 'NLP']\ncategory: ['ML & Deep Learning', 'Transformers']\nexcerpt: 'Batch Normalization fails for variable-length sequences. Layer Normalization fixes this by normalizing each token across its own features — exact math inside.'\nstatus: 'draft'\n---\n\n![Layer Normalization animation: BN failure on variable-length sequences, then LN step-by-step normalization of the \"big\" token](../Assets/blogs/layer-normalization-animation.mp4)\n_Watch BN fail when a short sequence leaves a position undefined, then see Layer Normalization normalize \"big\" step by step — mean subtracted, variance scaled, output confirmed zero-mean unit-variance._\n\n![BN vs LN: same formula, different axis of normalization](../Assets/blogs/layer-normalization-overview.png)\n_Batch Normalization normalizes each feature across the batch — undefined when sequences have different lengths. Layer Normalization normalizes each token across its own features, independently of every other token._\n\n## The Deeper You Go, the More the Ground Shifts\n\nBefore getting to Layer Normalization itself, it is worth understanding why normalization inside a neural network is necessary at all.\n\nConsider a network with six layers. You update the parameters of layer two during a gradient step. That update shifts the distribution of layer two's outputs — which are layer three's inputs. Layer three now receives inputs with a different mean and variance than it was trained to expect. It compensates by adjusting its own parameters, which shifts layer four's inputs, which propagates all the way down. Every weight update in an early layer quietly destabilizes every layer that follows it.\n\n[Ioffe and Szegedy (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167) named this phenomenon **internal covariate shift** — \"the change in the distributions of internal nodes of a deep network, in the course of training.\" The deeper the network, the more severe it gets. Training becomes a game of whack-a-mole: you fix one layer's distribution and the next one drifts.\n\nThe practical consequence is visible in the training curves. Without any normalization, deep networks demand very small learning rates — if you step too aggressively, an early-layer update cascades into instability in later layers. Training is slow, sensitive to initialization, and prone to vanishing or exploding gradients in the deepest layers.\n\n## What Batch Normalization Does — and Where It Cracks\n\nBatch Normalization was the dominant solution for four years, and it works well for the problem it was designed for: convolutional networks on fixed-size image batches.\n\nThe idea is to normalize each feature dimension across the mini-batch. For a batch of $B$ images, each with feature dimension $d$, Batch Normalization computes, for every dimension $k$:\n\n$$\\hat{x}^{(k)} = \\frac{x^{(k)} - \\mu_B^{(k)}}{\\sqrt{\\sigma_B^{(k)2} + \\varepsilon}}$$\n\nwhere $\\mu_B^{(k)}$ and $\\sigma_B^{(k)2}$ are the mean and variance of feature $k$ measured across the $B$ samples in the batch. Then it re-scales with learnable parameters:\n\n$$y^{(k)} = \\gamma^{(k)} \\hat{x}^{(k)} + \\beta^{(k)}$$\n\nFor images, this is sensible. Every image in the batch has the same spatial dimensions, so \"the first pixel of every image\" is a coherent statistical population. Batch statistics are stable and informative.\n\nSequences break this assumption in three distinct ways.\n\n**Variable length.** Natural language sequences have different lengths — \"cat sat\" is three tokens; \"the trophy was given to the boy because he earned it\" is fifteen. To apply Batch Normalization to sequences, you would need to compute statistics for each position across the batch. But position 10 simply does not exist in a three-token sequence. There is no meaningful value to contribute to the batch mean at that position. The authors of Layer Normalization state this directly: \"it is not obvious how to apply [batch normalization] to recurrent neural networks\" precisely because of this structural mismatch.\n\n**Small batches.** Batch statistics estimated from four or eight samples are noisy. With $B = 4$, the sample mean at any given feature dimension can be far from the true mean, and the sample variance will have high variance of its own. The normalization that was supposed to stabilize training instead injects noise.\n\n**Training–inference mismatch.** At inference time, you often process one sequence at a time — batch size one. Batch Normalization cannot compute meaningful statistics from a single sample, so it falls back to using running averages of $\\mu$ and $\\sigma$ accumulated during training. The network now behaves differently during inference than it did during training. [Ba et al. (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06450) put this cleanly: \"unlike batch normalization, layer normalization performs exactly the same computation at training and test times.\"\n\n## Layer Normalization: Normalize the Token, Not the Batch\n\nThe fix is to change which axis you normalize along. Instead of normalizing each feature across the batch, normalize all features within a single token.\n\nFor a token with embedding vector $\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_{\\text{model}}}$, Layer Normalization computes:\n\n$$\\mu = \\frac{1}{d_{\\text{model}}} \\sum_{i=1}^{d_{\\text{model}}} x_i$$\n\n$$\\sigma^2 = \\frac{1}{d_{\\text{model}}} \\sum_{i=1}^{d_{\\text{model}}} (x_i - \\mu)^2$$\n\n$$\\hat{x}_i = \\frac{x_i - \\mu}{\\sqrt{\\sigma^2 + \\varepsilon}}$$\n\n$$\\text{LN}(\\mathbf{x})_i = \\gamma_i \\hat{x}_i + \\beta_i$$\n\nThe mean $\\mu$ and variance $\\sigma^2$ are computed entirely from the $d_{\\text{model}}$ features of that one token. No other token is involved. No other sequence is involved. No batch is involved.\n\nThe learnable parameters $\\gamma \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_{\\text{model}}}$ (scale, initialized to 1) and $\\beta \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_{\\text{model}}}$ (shift, initialized to 0) give the network the freedom to undo the normalization if the task requires it. Without $\\gamma$ and $\\beta$, you would be forcing every layer's output to have unit variance, which might not be what the network needs. The learnable parameters restore expressivity after the stabilizing normalization.\n\nThe scalar $\\varepsilon$ — typically $10^{-5}$ — is added inside the square root for numerical stability. If all features of a token happened to be identical, $\\sigma^2 = 0$ and you would divide by zero. $\\varepsilon$ prevents that.\n\n## Worked Example: Normalizing \"big\" Step by Step\n\nThis series has used the sentence \"trophy was big\" as a running example. The self-attention post computed attention weights for each token; the multi-head attention post ran two independent heads over that sentence. By the time a token's representation reaches Layer Normalization, it carries the output of multi-head attention — a $d_{\\text{model}}$-dimensional vector.\n\nSay the \"big\" token's post-attention embedding is:\n\n$$\\mathbf{x}_{\\text{big}} = [1.0,\\ 3.0,\\ {-1.0},\\ 1.0], \\quad d_{\\text{model}} = 4$$\n\n**Step 1 — Compute the mean.**\n\n$$\\mu = \\frac{1.0 + 3.0 + (-1.0) + 1.0}{4} = \\frac{4.0}{4} = 1.0$$\n\n**Step 2 — Compute the variance.**\n\nEach term is $(x_i - \\mu)^2$:\n\n$$\\sigma^2 = \\frac{(1.0-1.0)^2 + (3.0-1.0)^2 + (-1.0-1.0)^2 + (1.0-1.0)^2}{4}$$\n\n$$= \\frac{0 + 4 + 4 + 0}{4} = \\frac{8}{4} = 2.0$$\n\n**Step 3 — Compute the standard deviation.**\n\n$$\\sigma = \\sqrt{\\sigma^2 + \\varepsilon} = \\sqrt{2.0 + 10^{-5}} \\approx 1.4142$$\n\n(The $\\varepsilon$ term is negligible here since $\\sigma^2$ is far from zero.)\n\n**Step 4 — Normalize each dimension.**\n\n$$\\hat{x}_0 = \\frac{1.0 - 1.0}{1.4142} = 0.000$$\n\n$$\\hat{x}_1 = \\frac{3.0 - 1.0}{1.4142} = \\frac{2.0}{1.4142} = 1.414$$\n\n$$\\hat{x}_2 = \\frac{-1.0 - 1.0}{1.4142} = \\frac{-2.0}{1.4142} = -1.414$$\n\n$$\\hat{x}_3 = \\frac{1.0 - 1.0}{1.4142} = 0.000$$\n\nSo $\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}_{\\text{big}} = [0.000,\\ 1.414,\\ {-1.414},\\ 0.000]$.\n\n**Step 5 — Scale and shift.**\n\nWith $\\gamma = [1, 1, 1, 1]$ and $\\beta = [0, 0, 0, 0]$ (the initialization values before any training), the output equals the normalized vector:\n\n$$\\text{LN}(\\mathbf{x}_{\\text{big}}) = [0.000,\\ 1.414,\\ {-1.414},\\ 0.000]$$\n\n**Verify.** The output should have mean 0 and variance 1:\n\n$$\\mu_{\\text{out}} = \\frac{0 + 1.414 + (-1.414) + 0}{4} = 0.0 \\checkmark$$\n\n$$\\sigma^2_{\\text{out}} = \\frac{0^2 + 1.414^2 + (-1.414)^2 + 0^2}{4} = \\frac{0 + 2 + 2 + 0}{4} = 1.0 \\checkmark$$\n\nThe general principle: Layer Normalization maps any token embedding — regardless of its original scale — to a vector with mean zero and variance one, then lets the network re-scale it with learned $\\gamma$ and $\\beta$.\n\n![Layer Normalization computation for the \"big\" token, step by step](../Assets/blogs/layer-normalization-computation.png)\n_Every step of the computation for $\\mathbf{x}_{\\text{big}} = [1.0, 3.0, -1.0, 1.0]$: subtract mean (1.0), divide by standard deviation (√2 ≈ 1.414), apply scale and shift — output has mean 0 and variance 1.\\_\n\n## Where Layer Norm Sits in the Transformer Block\n\nThe original [Vaswani et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) Transformer placed Layer Normalization _after_ the residual addition — a configuration now called **Post-LN**:\n\n$$\\mathbf{x}' = \\text{LayerNorm}(\\mathbf{x} + \\text{Sublayer}(\\mathbf{x}))$$\n\nThis is what the \"Attention Is All You Need\" paper shows in Figure 1. It works, but it has a stability problem. At initialization, when the sublayer weights are small random values, the output of the sublayer is approximately zero, so $\\mathbf{x} + \\text{Sublayer}(\\mathbf{x}) \\approx \\mathbf{x}$. The LayerNorm then normalizes $\\mathbf{x}$ directly. Gradients must flow backward through LayerNorm at every layer, and for deep networks this creates a vanishing gradient problem that makes Post-LN models require careful learning rate warmup schedules to survive the first few thousand steps.\n\nModern practice has moved to **Pre-LN**, used in GPT-2, LLaMA, Gemma, and most large-scale models released after 2019:\n\n$$\\mathbf{x}' = \\mathbf{x} + \\text{Sublayer}(\\text{LayerNorm}(\\mathbf{x}))$$\n\nThe residual connection now bypasses LayerNorm entirely. Gradients flow straight back through the addition without passing through any normalization. [Xiong et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745) proved formally that Pre-LN has better-behaved gradients at initialization and confirmed empirically that it trains stably without warmup. The cost is a small shift in how the model uses its representational capacity — the final output of a Pre-LN stack is not normalized, so a LayerNorm is typically added just before the output projection.\n\nThe distinction matters for the full Transformer block. One complete encoder layer applies two sublayers — multi-head self-attention followed by a position-wise feed-forward network — each wrapped in a residual + LayerNorm:\n\n$$\\mathbf{h} = \\text{LayerNorm}(\\mathbf{x} + \\text{MultiHeadAttention}(\\mathbf{x}))$$\n$$\\mathbf{x}' = \\text{LayerNorm}(\\mathbf{h} + \\text{FFN}(\\mathbf{h}))$$\n\n(Post-LN form, as in the original paper.) In the next post in this series, we will assemble all the pieces — self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encodings, and Layer Normalization — into the complete Transformer encoder block and trace a full forward pass from raw token IDs to contextualized embeddings.\n\n## Code\n\n```python\nimport torch\nimport torch.nn as nn\n\n# ── PyTorch built-in ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n# normalized_shape is the shape of the features to normalize over.\n# For a Transformer with d_model=512, use LayerNorm(512).\nln = nn.LayerNorm(normalized_shape=4)  # d_model=4 for our example\n\n# ── Manual implementation — matches the worked example exactly ────────────────\ndef layer_norm(x: torch.Tensor,\n               gamma: torch.Tensor,\n               beta: torch.Tensor,\n               eps: float = 1e-5) -> torch.Tensor:\n    \"\"\"\n    Layer Normalization for a single token embedding (or a batch of them).\n    Normalizes over the last dimension (feature dimension).\n\n    Args:\n        x:     (..., d_model) input tensor\n        gamma: (d_model,) learnable scale — initialized to 1\n        beta:  (d_model,) learnable shift — initialized to 0\n        eps:   small constant for numerical stability\n    \"\"\"\n    mean = x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)               # μ\n    var  = x.var(dim=-1, unbiased=False, keepdim=True) # σ²  (biased, like the paper)\n    x_hat = (x - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + eps)         # x̂\n    return gamma * x_hat + beta                        # γx̂ + β\n\n# ── Reproduce the \"big\" token example ────────────────────────────────────────\nx_big = torch.tensor([1.0, 3.0, -1.0, 1.0])\ngamma = torch.ones(4)    # γ: initialized to 1 (identity scale)\nbeta  = torch.zeros(4)   # β: initialized to 0 (no shift)\n\nout = layer_norm(x_big, gamma, beta)\nprint(out)\n# tensor([ 0.0000,  1.4142, -1.4142,  0.0000])\n\n# ── What happens after learning ───────────────────────────────────────────────\n# After training, γ and β are no longer identity/zero.\n# The network learns which feature dimensions should be amplified or suppressed.\ngamma_trained = torch.tensor([0.5, 2.0, 0.8, 1.5])\nbeta_trained  = torch.tensor([0.1, -0.3, 0.0, 0.2])\nout_trained = layer_norm(x_big, gamma_trained, beta_trained)\nprint(out_trained)\n# tensor([ 0.1000,  2.5284, -1.1314,  0.2000])\n# No longer zero-mean — the network re-centered it deliberately.\n```\n\nOne detail worth noting: PyTorch's `nn.LayerNorm` uses `unbiased=False` variance (divides by $N$, not $N-1$). That matches the paper. If you use `torch.var` directly, the default is `unbiased=True` (divides by $N-1$) — pass `unbiased=False` to match.\n\n## Failure Modes and Limitations\n\n**Small $d_{\\text{model}}$.** Layer Normalization estimates mean and variance from $d_{\\text{model}}$ numbers. For a $d_{\\text{model}} = 64$ model, that is 64 samples per estimate — adequate. For a tiny experimental model with $d_{\\text{model}} = 8$, the statistics are noisy, and the normalization can hurt more than it helps. Batch Normalization — when it is applicable — benefits from larger effective sample sizes.\n\n**Layer Norm can mask useful scale information.** The whole point of LayerNorm is to strip scale from the activations. If the magnitude of a token's representation is itself a signal the network should use (some argue this is the case in certain architectures), LayerNorm discards it. The learnable $\\gamma$ can in principle recover useful scaling, but it does so uniformly across all inputs — it cannot amplify a scale that varies meaningfully between tokens.\n\n**RMSNorm: the common simplification.** In practice, the mean-centering step ($x_i - \\mu$) turns out to contribute little to training stability. The dominant benefit comes from normalizing by the root-mean-square (RMS) of the activations, not from centering. This led to **Root Mean Square Layer Normalization (RMSNorm)**:\n\n$$\\text{RMSNorm}(\\mathbf{x})_i = \\frac{x_i}{\\sqrt{\\frac{1}{d}\\sum_j x_j^2 + \\varepsilon}} \\cdot \\gamma_i$$\n\nNo mean subtraction, no $\\beta$ shift parameter. Slightly cheaper to compute, and it performs comparably to full Layer Normalization in practice. LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral, and most recent large language models use RMSNorm rather than full Layer Normalization. If you are reading a model card and see \"RMSNorm,\" it is a stripped-down Layer Norm, not a fundamentally different idea.\n\n**Pre-LN vs. Post-LN — the practical summary.** If you are training a Transformer from scratch today, use Pre-LN. It trains stably without warmup, and modern evidence ([Xiong et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745)) consistently favors it over Post-LN for deep models. Post-LN is the original formulation, and you will see it in code that follows the 2017 paper closely, but it is not the default for new work.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Ba, Lei, Kiros, and Hinton — \"Layer Normalization\" (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06450)\n- [Ioffe and Szegedy — \"Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training\" (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167)\n- [Vaswani et al. — \"Attention Is All You Need\" (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)\n- [Xiong et al. — \"On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture\" (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745)\n- [Zhang and Sennrich — \"Root Mean Square Layer Normalization\" (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467)\n";
