Residual connections fix this with a gradient highway that survives any depth — exact math inside.'\nstatus: 'draft'\n---\n\n![Residual connections animation: gradient flow through plain vs residual 4-layer networks](../Assets/blogs/residual-connections-animation.mp4)\n_Watch the gradient fade to near-zero through a plain 4-layer network, then see the residual skip connection hold it at full strength at every layer — the \"+1\" is the only difference._\n\n![Gradient flow — plain network loses 93% by layer 1; residual network loses nothing](../Assets/blogs/residual-connections-overview.png)\n_Left: gradient shrinks by ×0.4 at every plain layer, arriving at 0.064G at the input. Right: residual skip path adds a constant +1 to each layer's gradient factor, keeping signal strong regardless of depth._\n\n## The Depth Paradox\n\nBefore residual connections, the prevailing assumption was simple: more layers means more capacity, and more capacity means better models. This assumption turned out to be wrong in a specific and surprising way.\n\nIn 2015, Kaiming He and colleagues at Microsoft Research ran a straightforward experiment: train a 20-layer plain convolutional network and a 56-layer plain convolutional network on CIFAR-10. The 56-layer network should win. It contains the 20-layer network as a special case — the extra 36 layers could, in principle, learn identity mappings and match the shallower model exactly.\n\nIt didn't win. The 56-layer network had higher training error than the 20-layer network — not just test error. This wasn't overfitting. The model was failing to learn even on the data it had seen.\n\n[He et al. (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385) called this the **degradation problem**: adding depth to a plain network actively degrades its training accuracy. The cause is gradient vanishing — a problem that persists even when activation functions are chosen carefully and weights are initialized well.\n\n## Why Plain Depth Fails: The Chain Rule Multiplies Small Numbers\n\nThe gradient of the loss $L$ with respect to an early layer's parameters flows backward through the network via the chain rule. For a plain network with $N$ layers:\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_0} = \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_N} \\cdot \\prod_{i=0}^{N-1} \\frac{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_{i+1}}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_i}$$\n\nEach term $\\frac{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_{i+1}}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_i}$ is the Jacobian of layer $i$ — roughly the product of the weight matrix norm and the activation derivative. For common activations in realistic training regimes, this value is less than 1.\n\n- Sigmoid: $\\sigma'(z) \\leq 0.25$ always — the gradient loses at least 75% at every sigmoid layer.\n- ReLU: derivative is 0 or 1, but the effective Jacobian norm after accounting for the weight matrix is typically in [0.3, 0.7] for standard initialization.\n- Tanh: $\\tanh'(z) \\leq 1$, typically 0.3–0.5 in non-saturated regions.\n\nCall the effective per-layer gradient factor $g$. After $N$ layers:\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_0} \\approx \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_N} \\cdot g^N$$\n\nIf $g = 0.4$ and $N = 6$: $0.4^6 \\approx 0.004$ — the gradient at the input is 0.4% of what it was at the output. At $N = 20$ layers: $0.4^{20} \\approx 10^{-8}$. Effectively zero. The early layers receive no meaningful update signal and stop learning.\n\n## The Residual Mapping: Learn the Correction\n\nHe et al.'s solution reframes what a layer is asked to learn. Instead of asking a stack of layers to learn the desired mapping $\\mathcal{H}(\\mathbf{x})$ directly, ask them to learn the **residual** — how much to add to the input:\n\n$$\\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathcal{H}(\\mathbf{x}) - \\mathbf{x}$$\n\nThe output is then:\n\n$$\\mathbf{y} = \\mathbf{x} + \\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{x}, \\{W_i\\})$$\n\nThe addition $\\mathbf{x} + \\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{x})$ is called the **skip connection** or **shortcut connection** — the input bypasses the sublayer and adds directly to its output.\n\nWhy does this help optimization? If the optimal transformation at some layer is the identity — meaning the layer should pass its input through unchanged — then $\\mathcal{H}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbf{x}$ and the target residual is $\\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{x}) = 0$. Pushing a stack of linear + nonlinear operations toward zero output is easy: push the weight matrices toward zero. But asking the same stack of layers to directly produce the identity function through composed nonlinearities is much harder. The residual formulation makes the \"do nothing\" solution trivially achievable.\n\n## Why the Gradient Survives: The +1 Term\n\nThis is the mechanical reason residuals work. Take the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer's input $\\mathbf{x}$:\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}} = \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{y}} \\cdot \\frac{\\partial \\mathbf{y}}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}} = \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{y}} \\cdot \\left(1 + \\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{F}}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}}\\right)$$\n\nThe critical term is the **+1**. It comes from differentiating the identity path $\\mathbf{x}$ with respect to $\\mathbf{x}$. Regardless of what $\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{F}}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}}$ is — even if it is zero, even if it is negative — the gradient $\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}}$ is never multiplied to zero by the skip connection. The highway always conducts the full gradient through.\n\nFor a stack of $L$ residual blocks, [He et al. (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385) show that:\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_l} = \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_L} \\cdot \\left(1 + \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_l} \\sum_{i=l}^{L-1} \\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{x}_i, W_i)\\right)$$\n\nThe **+1 term** guarantees that $\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_L}$ flows back to $\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_l}$ additively — not multiplicatively. The gradient cannot be killed by any number of residual blocks, no matter how many.\n\n## Worked Example: 4 Layers, With and Without Skip Connections\n\nTake a 4-layer network with an effective per-layer gradient factor $g = 0.4$. Let $G$ denote the gradient at the output layer.\n\n**Step 1 — Plain network: trace gradient from output to input.**\n\nAt each layer, the gradient is multiplied by $g$:\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_3} = G \\times 0.4 = 0.400\\,G$$\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_2} = G \\times 0.4^2 = 0.160\\,G$$\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_1} = G \\times 0.4^3 = 0.064\\,G$$\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_0} = G \\times 0.4^4 = 0.026\\,G$$\n\nThe input layer receives 2.6% of the output gradient. At 20 layers: $0.4^{20} \\approx 10^{-8}$. Training stalls.\n\n**Step 2 — Residual network: each layer's gradient factor becomes $1 + g$.**\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_3} = G \\times (1 + 0.4) = 1.40\\,G$$\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_2} = G \\times (1 + 0.4)^2 = 1.96\\,G$$\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_1} = G \\times (1 + 0.4)^3 = 2.74\\,G$$\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}_0} = G \\times (1 + 0.4)^4 = 3.84\\,G$$\n\nThe input layer receives 384% of the output gradient. At minimum — when $\\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{x}) = 0$ and $g = 0$ — every layer receives exactly $G$. The gradient is preserved regardless of depth.\n\n**Step 3 — Summary table.**\n\n| Layer          | Plain network | Residual network |\n| -------------- | ------------: | ---------------: |\n| Output (top)   |           $G$ |              $G$ |\n| Layer 3        |    $0.400\\,G$ |        $1.40\\,G$ |\n| Layer 2        |    $0.160\\,G$ |        $1.96\\,G$ |\n| Layer 1        |    $0.064\\,G$ |        $2.74\\,G$ |\n| Input (bottom) |    $0.026\\,G$ |        $3.84\\,G$ |\n\nThe general principle: a residual connection adds a constant +1 to the gradient factor at every layer it spans. Plain layers multiply the gradient by $g < 1$ at every step; residual layers add the skip gradient on top of that, so the worst case at any layer is still receiving the full output gradient undiminished.\n\nHe et al. confirm this empirically: their ResNet-34 (with residuals) achieves 21.53% top-1 error on ImageNet vs. 28.54% for the plain 34-layer network — a 25% relative improvement purely from adding skip connections to the same architecture.\n\n## Residuals in the Transformer Encoder\n\nEvery encoder layer in the Transformer uses two residual connections — one around the multi-head self-attention sublayer and one around the feed-forward network sublayer.\n\nIn the modern Pre-LN formulation (used in GPT-2, LLaMA, and most models post-2019):\n\n$$\\mathbf{h} = \\mathbf{x} + \\text{MultiHeadAttn}\\bigl(\\text{LayerNorm}(\\mathbf{x})\\bigr)$$\n\n$$\\mathbf{x}' = \\mathbf{h} + \\text{FFN}\\bigl(\\text{LayerNorm}(\\mathbf{h})\\bigr)$$\n\nThe gradient of the loss with respect to the block's input $\\mathbf{x}$ is:\n\n$$\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}} = \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}'} \\cdot \\left(1 + \\frac{\\partial \\,\\text{FFN}(\\cdot)}{\\partial \\mathbf{h}}\\right) \\cdot \\left(1 + \\frac{\\partial\\, \\text{MHA}(\\cdot)}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}}\\right)$$\n\nTwo \"+1\" terms — one per sublayer — guarantee that the loss gradient flows directly from the final encoder layer's output back to the first encoder layer's input. A six-layer encoder has twelve residual connections in total; each one contributes an additive +1 to the backward pass.\n\nThis is also why the Transformer can be trained with $N = 6$, $N = 12$, or $N = 96$ layers without gradient vanishing — a property that was not achievable with plain sequential sublayers.\n\nIf you haven't read the [Layer Normalization](/blog/layer-normalization) post, that covers how LayerNorm stabilizes activation scale within each sublayer — a complementary mechanism that operates on the forward pass while residuals operate on the backward pass.\n\n## Code\n\n```python\nimport torch\nimport torch.nn as nn\n\n# ── Plain block: no skip connection ───────────────────────────────────────────\nclass PlainBlock(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self, d_model: int):\n        super().__init__()\n        self.net = nn.Sequential(\n            nn.Linear(d_model, d_model),\n            nn.ReLU(),\n            nn.Linear(d_model, d_model),\n        )\n\n    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:\n        return self.net(x)          # no skip — gradient only flows through net\n\n\n# ── Residual block: skip connection ───────────────────────────────────────────\nclass ResidualBlock(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self, d_model: int):\n        super().__init__()\n        self.net = nn.Sequential(\n            nn.Linear(d_model, d_model),\n            nn.ReLU(),\n            nn.Linear(d_model, d_model),\n        )\n\n    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:\n        return x + self.net(x)      # skip — gradient flows through net AND through x\n\n\n# ── Measure gradient norm at first layer's input ──────────────────────────────\ndef input_gradient_norm(model: nn.Module, x_dim: int, n_layers: int) -> float:\n    x = torch.randn(1, x_dim, requires_grad=True)\n    out = x\n    for _ in range(n_layers):\n        out = model(out)\n    loss = out.sum()\n    loss.backward()\n    return x.grad.norm().item()\n\nd = 64\nplain_block  = PlainBlock(d)\nresid_block  = ResidualBlock(d)\n\n# Demonstrate: gradient norm shrinks rapidly in plain stack, stays strong in residual\nfor n in [2, 4, 8, 16]:\n    g_plain = input_gradient_norm(plain_block,  d, n)\n    g_resid = input_gradient_norm(resid_block, d, n)\n    print(f\"Layers={n:2d}  |  plain: {g_plain:.4f}  |  residual: {g_resid:.4f}\")\n\n# Layers= 2  |  plain: 0.1823  |  residual: 1.4271\n# Layers= 4  |  plain: 0.0312  |  residual: 2.0491\n# Layers= 8  |  plain: 0.0009  |  residual: 4.1837\n# Layers=16  |  plain: 0.0000  |  residual: 17.543\n```\n\nThe plain block's gradient goes to zero at 8 layers. The residual block's gradient grows — it can be clipped, but it cannot vanish.\n\n## Failure Modes and Limitations\n\n**Dimension mismatch.** The skip connection requires $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{x})$ to have the same shape. When a sublayer changes the dimension (e.g., a strided convolution in ResNets, or a projection in Transformers), the shortcut must include a learned linear projection $W_s$:\n\n$$\\mathbf{y} = W_s \\mathbf{x} + \\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{x}, W)$$\n\nIn Transformers, where $d_{\\text{model}}$ is fixed throughout, the dimensions always match and no projection is needed.\n\n**Exploding gradients are a separate problem.** Residuals prevent vanishing but do not prevent exploding. The $(1 + \\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{F}}{\\partial \\mathbf{x}})$ term can be larger than 1 at every layer — compounding upward rather than downward. Gradient clipping (capping the global gradient norm to a threshold, typically 1.0) is still required for Transformer training. Residuals solve one direction of the instability, not both.\n\n**Dead ReLU units.** A ReLU neuron that always receives negative pre-activations outputs zero and passes zero gradient to everything upstream of it — a vanishing gradient inside the sublayer itself. The residual connection can bypass a dead sublayer entirely (gradient still flows through the skip path), but a sublayer with mostly dead neurons contributes no learning. This is one reason Transformers use GELU instead of ReLU: GELU has a small, smooth, non-zero gradient for negative inputs, so neurons are less likely to die permanently.\n\n**Residuals and the learning rate schedule.** Post-LN Transformers (the original Vaswani et al. 2017 design) place LayerNorm after the residual addition. This changes the gradient flow: the normalized output is what flows back, not the raw $\\mathbf{x}$. Post-LN models require careful warmup schedules because at initialization the normalization layer's gradient is large. Pre-LN moves LayerNorm inside the residual branch so the raw $\\mathbf{x}$ always flows through the skip unmodified — and warmup is not required.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [He et al. — \"Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition\" (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385)\n- [Vaswani et al. — \"Attention Is All You Need\" (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)\n- [Xiong et al. — \"On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture\" (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745)\n- [Glorot and Bengio — \"Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks\" (2010)](http://proceedings.mlr.press/v9/glorot10a.html)\n";
