export default "---\ntitle: 'Self-Attention from First Principles: Why RNNs Had to Die'\ndate: '2024-10-24'\nslug: 'self-attention-from-first-principles'\ntags: ['Deep Learning', 'Transformers', 'Self-Attention', 'NLP']\ncategory: ['ML & Deep Learning', 'Transformers']\nexcerpt: 'RNNs compress entire sequences into one fixed vector. Self-attention replaces that bottleneck with direct token-to-token communication — here is how it works.'\nstatus: 'draft'\n---\n\n![Self-attention animation: the RNN overwrites \"trophy\" by the time it reaches \"it\" — then self-attention shows \"it\" querying all tokens in one pass and attending most strongly to \"trophy\" (0.412)](../Assets/blogs/attention-animation.mp4)\n\n_Watch \"trophy\" fade in the RNN's hidden state as tokens overwrite it. Then self-attention: \"it\" sends a query to every token simultaneously and the highest score lands on \"trophy\" — no bottleneck, no overwriting._\n\n![RNN sequential bottleneck vs self-attention direct communication](../Assets/blogs/self-attention-rnn-vs-attention.png)\n\n_Left: an RNN compresses the entire sequence into a single hidden vector — \"trophy\" information fades through 7 sequential overwrites before \"it\" can use it. Right: self-attention lets every token communicate directly with every other in one pass._\n\n## The Problem Self-Attention Was Designed to Fix\n\n\"The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big.\" You read that and without hesitation you know \"it\" refers to the trophy. Suitcases don't fail to contain themselves. The resolution requires connecting position 9 (\"it\") back to position 2 (\"trophy\"), hopping over a causal clause and seven intervening tokens.\n\nConsider what a recurrent neural network does with this sentence. It processes tokens one at a time, left to right. At step 2, \"trophy\" updates the hidden state $h_2$. At step 3, \"didn't\" overwrites part of $h_2$ to produce $h_3$. By the time the model reaches \"it\" at step 9, the hidden state $h_9$ is a compression of everything that came before — \"trophy,\" \"suitcase,\" the negation, the causal connector — squeezed into a fixed-size vector through eight successive nonlinear transformations. Whether $h_9$ still carries enough signal about \"trophy\" to resolve the pronoun correctly depends on whether the LSTM's forget gate happened to preserve it. Sometimes it does. Frequently, for long sentences, it doesn't.\n\n[Bahdanau et al. (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473) measured this directly: performance of the RNN encoder-decoder \"dramatically drops as the length of the sentences increases.\" The bottleneck is architectural, not a matter of training harder or longer.\n\n[Cho et al. (2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.1078) had designed the encoder-decoder cleanly: \"one RNN encodes a sequence of symbols into a fixed-length vector representation, and the other decodes the representation into another sequence of symbols.\" It was a good design for short sentences. Bahdanau et al. then pointed at precisely what that design required: \"a neural network needs to be able to compress all the necessary information of a source sentence into a fixed-length vector.\" They called it a \"bottleneck,\" and they were right. Their fix was to let the decoder look back at all encoder hidden states directly, weighting each by learned relevance, rather than working from a single compressed summary. That alignment mechanism was the seed of attention.\n\nSelf-attention takes the same idea and applies it within a single sequence, to every token simultaneously. No recurrence. No fixed-size bottleneck. Every token can attend to every other token in one pass.\n\n## What \"Attend\" Actually Means\n\nBefore any math, the intuition. When you read \"trophy,\" you form some representation — a physical object, probably gold-colored, heavy, given as an award. When you later read \"big,\" you implicitly connect it back to the trophy — because \"big\" is a size descriptor, and trophies are the kind of thing that can be too big to fit somewhere. That connection, made effortlessly by human readers, is what attention formalizes.\n\nSelf-attention gives each token three different projections of itself:\n\nA **query** (Q) — what this token is looking for in other tokens.\nA **key** (K) — what this token offers to match other tokens' queries.\nA **value** (V) — the actual information this token contributes if selected.\n\nThe query and key interact by dot product. If $\\mathbf{q}_i \\cdot \\mathbf{k}_j$ is large, tokens $i$ and $j$ are a good match. Those scores get normalized across all tokens, then used to compute a weighted mixture of all values. Each token's output is a new representation that blends context from every other token, weighted by how relevant they are.\n\nWhat makes this work is that Q, K, and V are all learned projections. The model learns, from data, what \"asking for a size-describable noun\" looks like in query space, what \"being a size-describable noun\" looks like in key space, and what information from that noun is worth passing downstream. No hand-coded rules. The structure emerges from training.\n\n![Q/K/V projection for the \"big\" token showing how one embedding projects into three separate vectors](../Assets/blogs/self-attention-qkv-projection.png)\n\n_The \"big\" token's embedding is projected through three independent weight matrices. W_Q extracts what \"big\" is looking for (adjective-ness + size-relatedness). W_K extracts what \"big\" offers to other queries. W_V holds the information \"big\" contributes to the final output mix._\n\n## Building It from Scratch\n\nThree tokens: **\"trophy was big\"**. Embeddings are 4-dimensional — tiny by any real standard (the Transformer paper uses 512), but enough to trace every number.\n\nImagine the 4 dimensions encode simple properties:\n\n| dim | meaning        |\n| --- | -------------- |\n| 0   | noun-like      |\n| 1   | verb-like      |\n| 2   | adjective-like |\n| 3   | size-related   |\n\nUnder this scheme:\n\n$$\\mathbf{x}_{\\text{trophy}} = [1, 0, 0, 1], \\quad \\mathbf{x}_{\\text{was}} = [0, 1, 0, 0], \\quad \\mathbf{x}_{\\text{big}} = [0, 0, 1, 1]$$\n\n\"trophy\" is a noun with a size dimension. \"was\" is a verb, nothing else. \"big\" is an adjective that's size-related.\n\nNow define three projection matrices, each $4 \\times 2$ — projecting embeddings down to $d_k = 2$:\n\n$$W_Q = \\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0\\\\0 & 0\\\\1 & 0\\\\0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}, \\quad W_K = \\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\\\0 & 0\\\\0 & 0\\\\0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}, \\quad W_V = \\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\\\0 & 1\\\\0 & 0\\\\0 & 0\\end{bmatrix}$$\n\n$W_Q$ extracts adjective-ness (dim 2) and size-relatedness (dim 3) from the query side — it captures what kind of thing is doing the looking. $W_K$ extracts noun-ness (dim 0) and size-capability (dim 3) — it captures what kind of thing can be pointed to as describable by size. $W_V$ extracts entity and action information for downstream use.\n\n**Step 1: Compute queries and keys.**\n\nQueries ($\\mathbf{Q} = \\mathbf{X} W_Q$, each row is one token's query vector):\n\n$$\\mathbf{q}_{\\text{trophy}} = [1,0,0,1]\\, W_Q = [0,\\; 1]$$\n$$\\mathbf{q}_{\\text{was}} = [0,1,0,0]\\, W_Q = [0,\\; 0]$$\n$$\\mathbf{q}_{\\text{big}} = [0,0,1,1]\\, W_Q = [1,\\; 1]$$\n\nKeys ($\\mathbf{K} = \\mathbf{X} W_K$):\n\n$$\\mathbf{k}_{\\text{trophy}} = [1,\\; 1], \\quad \\mathbf{k}_{\\text{was}} = [0,\\; 0], \\quad \\mathbf{k}_{\\text{big}} = [0,\\; 1]$$\n\n**Step 2: Attention scores for \"big\" as the query.**\n\n\"big\" asks, via $\\mathbf{q}_{\\text{big}} = [1, 1]$: \"I'm an adjective that's size-related — which token here is size-describable?\"\n\n$$e_{\\text{big} \\to \\text{trophy}} = \\mathbf{q}_{\\text{big}} \\cdot \\mathbf{k}_{\\text{trophy}} = [1,1] \\cdot [1,1] = 2$$\n$$e_{\\text{big} \\to \\text{was}} = \\mathbf{q}_{\\text{big}} \\cdot \\mathbf{k}_{\\text{was}} = [1,1] \\cdot [0,0] = 0$$\n$$e_{\\text{big} \\to \\text{big}} = \\mathbf{q}_{\\text{big}} \\cdot \\mathbf{k}_{\\text{big}} = [1,1] \\cdot [0,1] = 1$$\n\n**Step 3: Scale by $\\sqrt{d_k}$.**\n\nDivide by $\\sqrt{2} \\approx 1.414$:\n\n$$\\text{scaled} = [2/1.414,\\;\\; 0/1.414,\\;\\; 1/1.414] = [1.41,\\;\\; 0,\\;\\; 0.71]$$\n\n**Step 4: Softmax.**\n\n$$e^{1.41} \\approx 4.09, \\quad e^{0} = 1.00, \\quad e^{0.71} \\approx 2.03, \\quad \\text{sum} = 7.12$$\n\n$$\\alpha_{\\text{trophy}} \\approx 0.575, \\quad \\alpha_{\\text{was}} \\approx 0.140, \\quad \\alpha_{\\text{big}} \\approx 0.285$$\n\n\"big\" attends to \"trophy\" with weight 0.575. The verb \"was\" barely registers at 0.140. Without a single hard-coded rule about grammar, the mechanism learned — through the structure of the projection matrices — that a size adjective should look to nouns rather than verbs.\n\n![Attention weight matrix heatmap for the three-token sequence \"trophy was big\"](../Assets/blogs/self-attention-heatmap.png)\n\n_The full 3×3 attention weight matrix. Each row sums to 1. \"was\" produces uniform weights because its key vector is all zeros — every dot product is zero, softmax gives equal weight. The green box highlights the \"big\" row: it attends most strongly to \"trophy\" (0.576), confirming the mechanism found the adjective–noun relationship without any explicit grammar rules._\n\n**Step 5: Compute values and mix.**\n\n$$\\mathbf{v}_{\\text{trophy}} = [1,0,0,1]\\, W_V = [1,\\; 0]$$\n$$\\mathbf{v}_{\\text{was}} = [0,1,0,0]\\, W_V = [0,\\; 1]$$\n$$\\mathbf{v}_{\\text{big}} = [0,0,1,1]\\, W_V = [0,\\; 0]$$\n\n$$\\mathbf{o}_{\\text{big}} = 0.575 \\cdot [1,0] + 0.140 \\cdot [0,1] + 0.285 \\cdot [0,0] = [0.575,\\;\\; 0.140]$$\n\nThe output for \"big\" now carries substantial signal from the \"trophy\" entity (dim 0 = 0.575) and a small amount of verb context from \"was\" (dim 1 = 0.140). \"big\"'s original embedding contained zero noun information. Attention mixed it in.\n\nThis is the core operation: context-aware representation. Each token's output is a differentiable, learned, parallel-computed mixture of all tokens' values.\n\n## Why Divide by $\\sqrt{d_k}$?\n\nThe scaling is easy to treat as a detail. It's not.\n\nIf the components of $\\mathbf{q}$ and $\\mathbf{k}$ are each drawn independently from $\\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, their dot product $\\mathbf{q} \\cdot \\mathbf{k} = \\sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$ has mean 0 and variance $d_k$. Each product $q_i k_i$ has variance 1, and summing $d_k$ independent terms accumulates variance linearly. Standard deviation grows as $\\sqrt{d_k}$.\n\nWith the Transformer's base model using $d_k = 64$, raw dot products have standard deviation 8. So before softmax, scores might look like $[9.2,\\; -4.1,\\; 13.5,\\; -6.8,\\; \\ldots]$. After softmax, $e^{13.5}$ dominates so completely that one token absorbs nearly all the weight. The distribution collapses to near one-hot. The gradient through a near-one-hot softmax is vanishingly small — the model can't learn.\n\nDividing by $\\sqrt{d_k}$ normalizes variance back to 1, keeping scores in a range where softmax produces smooth gradients. The [Vaswani et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) paper puts it plainly: \"we suspect that for large values of $d_k$, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients.\"\n\nOne division. Makes high-dimensional attention trainable.\n\n## The General Formula\n\n$$\\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \\text{softmax}\\!\\left(\\frac{QK^\\top}{\\sqrt{d_k}}\\right)V$$\n\n$Q$, $K$, $V$ are matrices — each row is one token's query, key, or value. $QK^\\top$ produces an $n \\times n$ matrix of all pairwise dot products. After scaling and softmax, you get the attention weight matrix $\\alpha$, where $\\alpha_{ij}$ is how much token $i$ attends to token $j$. Multiplying by $V$ takes the weighted mixture.\n\nThe computation is $O(n^2 d)$ in time and $O(n^2)$ in memory. For 512 tokens that's 262,144 pairwise scores, which is fine. For 100K-token contexts that's 10 billion — which is why nearly every long-context architecture since 2020 is partly an attempt to approximate or avoid this matrix.\n\n## Code: Self-Attention from Scratch\n\n```python\nimport numpy as np\n\ndef softmax(x, axis=-1):\n    \"\"\"Numerically stable softmax along the specified axis.\"\"\"\n    x = x - np.max(x, axis=axis, keepdims=True)  # subtract max for stability\n    exp_x = np.exp(x)\n    return exp_x / np.sum(exp_x, axis=axis, keepdims=True)\n\ndef self_attention(X, W_Q, W_K, W_V):\n    \"\"\"\n    Scaled dot-product self-attention.\n\n    Args:\n        X:   (n, d_model)   token embeddings\n        W_Q: (d_model, d_k) query projection\n        W_K: (d_model, d_k) key projection\n        W_V: (d_model, d_v) value projection\n\n    Returns:\n        O: (n, d_v)  contextual output for each token\n        A: (n, n)    attention weight matrix\n    \"\"\"\n    d_k = W_Q.shape[1]\n\n    Q = X @ W_Q          # (n, d_k)\n    K = X @ W_K          # (n, d_k)\n    V = X @ W_V          # (n, d_v)\n\n    scores = (Q @ K.T) / np.sqrt(d_k)   # (n, n) scaled dot products\n    A = softmax(scores, axis=-1)         # row-wise softmax → attention weights\n    O = A @ V                            # (n, d_v) weighted value mixture\n\n    return O, A\n\n\n# ── Reproduce the worked example ──────────────────────────────────────────────\nX = np.array([\n    [1, 0, 0, 1],   # \"trophy\": noun, size-capable\n    [0, 1, 0, 0],   # \"was\":    verb\n    [0, 0, 1, 1],   # \"big\":    adjective, size-related\n], dtype=float)\n\n# W_Q extracts [adjective-ness, size-relatedness] — what is doing the asking\nW_Q = np.array([[0,0],[0,0],[1,0],[0,1]], dtype=float)\n# W_K extracts [noun-ness, size-capability] — what can be asked about\nW_K = np.array([[1,0],[0,0],[0,0],[0,1]], dtype=float)\n# W_V extracts [entity-info, action-info]\nW_V = np.array([[1,0],[0,1],[0,0],[0,0]], dtype=float)\n\nO, A = self_attention(X, W_Q, W_K, W_V)\n\ntokens = [\"trophy\", \"was\", \"big\"]\nprint(\"Attention weights (row = query token, col = key token):\")\nprint(f\"{'':>8}\", \" \".join(f\"{t:>8}\" for t in tokens))\nfor i, row in enumerate(A):\n    print(f\"{tokens[i]:>8}\", \" \".join(f\"{v:>8.3f}\" for v in row))\n\nprint(\"\\nOutput vectors:\")\nfor i, o in enumerate(O):\n    print(f\"  {tokens[i]}: {np.round(o, 3)}\")\n```\n\nRunning this reproduces the exact numbers from the worked example: \"big\" attends to \"trophy\" at 0.575. You can also inspect the full attention matrix — \"trophy\" attends mostly to itself (it's a subject; it doesn't need context from the other tokens under these toy projections), and \"was\" produces near-uniform attention because its key vector is all zeros, making every dot product zero, and softmax of uniform inputs is uniform.\n\n## What Self-Attention Still Cannot Do\n\nWorth being explicit about this, because the mechanism is often presented as a complete solution.\n\n**Position is invisible.** The computation above is fully permutation-invariant. Shuffle \"trophy was big\" into \"big trophy was\" and the mechanism produces different outputs because query-key pairings shift, but it has no inherent representation of which position any token occupies. The original Transformer paper adds sinusoidal position encodings to the input embeddings before computing attention. Without them, the model cannot distinguish \"cat bites dog\" from \"dog bites cat\" — they produce identical attention patterns.\n\n**Nonlinearity lives elsewhere.** Self-attention is a linear sequence of operations (matrix multiplications plus softmax, which is nonlinear but applied uniformly to scores, not to representations). The expressive depth of a Transformer comes from stacking attention layers with position-wise feed-forward networks — two linear layers with a ReLU between them — applied independently to each token. Self-attention mixes information across positions; the FFN transforms it. Remove either, and the architecture degrades.\n\n**The quadratic wall is real.** $n$ tokens means $n^2$ attention scores. This is the engineering constraint that motivated [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135) (recomputing attention blocks in SRAM to avoid writing the full matrix to HBM), sparse attention patterns, linear attention approximations, and state-space alternatives like [Mamba](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752). The quadratic cost isn't a design flaw — it's the price of computing all pairwise relationships exactly. Every efficient-attention paper is, in some sense, a negotiation over how much of that exactness to give up.\n\nSelf-attention handles context mixing. Positional encodings handle order. Feed-forward layers handle transformation. Multiple heads handle representational diversity. The Transformer is a set of cooperating components, not a single mechanism that does everything — and understanding where each boundary falls is what separates practitioners who use transformers from engineers who can reason about what goes wrong with them.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Attention Is All You Need — Vaswani et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)\n- [Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate — Bahdanau et al. (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473)\n- [Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder — Cho et al. (2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.1078)\n- [FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention — Dao et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)\n- [Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces — Gu & Dao (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752)\n";
