export default "---\ntitle: 'Positional Encodings: How the Transformer Knows Where Tokens Are'\ndate: '2024-11-3'\nslug: 'positional-encodings'\ntags: ['Deep Learning', 'Transformers', 'NLP', 'Positional Encoding']\ncategory: ['ML & Deep Learning', 'Transformers']\nexcerpt: 'Self-attention is blind to token order. Positional encodings fix that by injecting position as data — here is the exact math and why sinusoids work.'\nstatus: 'draft'\n---\n\n![Sinusoidal positional encoding heatmap: each row is one position's unique 64-dimensional fingerprint, with high-frequency oscillations in early dimensions and near-constant values in late dimensions](../Assets/blogs/positional-encodings-heatmap.png)\n_Each row is one token position's encoding vector. Early dimensions (left) oscillate fast — enough to distinguish adjacent tokens. Late dimensions (right) oscillate so slowly they barely change across 50 positions, but would cleanly distinguish position 0 from position 5,000. Together they create a unique fingerprint for every position at every scale._\n\n## Where We Left Off\n\nBoth [Self-Attention from First Principles](https://ankitkr8540.github.io/portfolio/#/blogs/self-attention-from-first-principles) and [Multi-Head Attention](https://ankitkr8540.github.io/portfolio/#/blogs/multi-head-attention) end with the same warning: self-attention is permutation-invariant. Shuffle \"trophy was big\" into \"big was trophy\" and the query, key, and value vectors are identical — only the row ordering changes. The attention weights shift because different tokens are now in different positions in the sequence matrix, but the mechanism itself has no notion of which token came first, second, or third.\n\nThat's not a minor limitation. \"The cat chased the dog\" and \"The dog chased the cat\" have the same tokens, completely different meanings, and identical self-attention inputs. Without positional information, the Transformer cannot tell them apart.\n\nThis post closes that gap: where the problem comes from, what a good solution requires, and why sinusoidal encodings are the specific answer [Vaswani et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) chose.\n\n## What RNNs Got For Free\n\nBefore self-attention, sequence models were recurrent — Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), vanilla RNN. These process tokens strictly left to right: at step $t$, the model reads token $t$ and updates a hidden state that carries forward everything seen so far.\n\nPosition was implicit. Token at step 3 is processed third. There was no need to tell the model where in the sequence it was — the computation order was the sequence order. The architectural bottleneck this created (the overwriting problem, the parallelism ceiling) was what motivated the Transformer in the first place, as covered in the self-attention post.\n\nThe Transformer's fix — process all tokens simultaneously with attention — breaks the implicit position encoding. Vaswani et al. state this bluntly in section 3.5: \"Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.\"\n\nInject. Position is no longer structurally guaranteed. It has to be added as data.\n\n## What a Good Positional Encoding Needs to Do\n\nBefore picking a specific function, it's worth pinning down what \"good\" means. A positional encoding scheme needs to satisfy four requirements — and not all obvious candidates satisfy all four.\n\n**Uniqueness.** Every position must map to a different encoding. If positions 3 and 7 have the same encoding, the model cannot distinguish them.\n\n**Consistent relative distances.** The geometric relationship between positions should be consistent. \"Two positions apart\" should feel the same whether you're looking at positions (0, 2) or positions (100, 102). The model shouldn't have to learn that \"far apart\" means different things at different absolute locations.\n\n**Generalization to unseen lengths.** A model trained on sequences up to length 512 might encounter length 600 at inference. The encoding scheme should produce meaningful values at positions it's never seen during training — not garbage or out-of-distribution noise.\n\n**Bounded values.** If positional encodings grow without bound, they'll dominate the token embeddings they're added to. The encoding values need to stay in a range comparable to the embedding values.\n\nSimple options fail obviously: integers (1, 2, 3, ...) satisfy uniqueness but grow without bound and don't generalize cleanly. Normalized positions (pos/seq_len) satisfy boundedness but aren't consistent across sequences of different lengths — position 0.5 means something different in a length-10 sequence than a length-100 sequence.\n\nSinusoidal functions satisfy all four. Here's why.\n\n## The Sinusoidal Solution\n\n[Vaswani et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) define the positional encoding for position $\\text{pos}$ and dimension index $d$ as:\n\n$$\\text{PE}(\\text{pos},\\, 2i) = \\sin\\!\\left(\\frac{\\text{pos}}{10000^{2i/d_{\\text{model}}}}\\right)$$\n\n$$\\text{PE}(\\text{pos},\\, 2i+1) = \\cos\\!\\left(\\frac{\\text{pos}}{10000^{2i/d_{\\text{model}}}}\\right)$$\n\nwhere $i = 0, 1, \\ldots, d_{\\text{model}}/2 - 1$ indexes the sine/cosine pair. Every even dimension gets a sine; every odd dimension gets a cosine. The denominator $10000^{2i/d_{\\text{model}}}$ is the wavelength scaling factor — call it $\\omega_i$.\n\n**Boundedness:** sine and cosine are bounded in $[-1, 1]$ at every position. Satisfied.\n\n**Uniqueness:** the $d_{\\text{model}}$ dimensions together form a pattern that is unique per position. Individually, a single dimension isn't unique — $\\sin(\\text{pos}/\\omega_i)$ repeats with period $2\\pi\\omega_i$. But across all $d_{\\text{model}}$ dimensions simultaneously, no two positions produce the same vector (for the positional range relevant to NLP tasks).\n\n**Consistent relative distances:** this is the deep property, and it comes from the angle addition formula. For any fixed offset $k$:\n\n$$\\text{PE}(\\text{pos}+k,\\, 2i) = \\sin\\!\\left(\\frac{\\text{pos}+k}{\\omega_i}\\right) = \\sin\\!\\left(\\frac{\\text{pos}}{\\omega_i}\\right)\\cos\\!\\left(\\frac{k}{\\omega_i}\\right) + \\cos\\!\\left(\\frac{\\text{pos}}{\\omega_i}\\right)\\sin\\!\\left(\\frac{k}{\\omega_i}\\right)$$\n\n$$\\text{PE}(\\text{pos}+k,\\, 2i+1) = \\cos\\!\\left(\\frac{\\text{pos}+k}{\\omega_i}\\right) = \\cos\\!\\left(\\frac{\\text{pos}}{\\omega_i}\\right)\\cos\\!\\left(\\frac{k}{\\omega_i}\\right) - \\sin\\!\\left(\\frac{\\text{pos}}{\\omega_i}\\right)\\sin\\!\\left(\\frac{k}{\\omega_i}\\right)$$\n\nWritten in matrix form, for any dimension pair $(2i, 2i+1)$:\n\n$$\\begin{bmatrix}\\text{PE}(\\text{pos}+k,\\, 2i) \\\\ \\text{PE}(\\text{pos}+k,\\, 2i+1)\\end{bmatrix} = \\begin{bmatrix}\\cos(k/\\omega_i) & \\sin(k/\\omega_i) \\\\ -\\sin(k/\\omega_i) & \\cos(k/\\omega_i)\\end{bmatrix} \\begin{bmatrix}\\text{PE}(\\text{pos},\\, 2i) \\\\ \\text{PE}(\\text{pos},\\, 2i+1)\\end{bmatrix}$$\n\nThe $2 \\times 2$ matrix on the right is a fixed rotation — it depends only on $k$ and $\\omega_i$, not on $\\text{pos}$ at all. \"Two steps ahead\" is always the same rotation, regardless of where you are in the sequence. The model can learn to recognize this rotation — and by doing so, learn to attend to tokens at a fixed relative offset without knowing absolute positions.\n\nThe paper's own reasoning: \"we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset $k$, $\\text{PE}(\\text{pos}+k)$ can be represented as a linear function of $\\text{PE}(\\text{pos})$.\"\n\n**Generalization:** sinusoidal functions are defined for any real-valued argument. PE(pos=1000) is as well-defined as PE(pos=5). Learned positional embeddings — a lookup table, one vector per position — cannot extrapolate past the training vocabulary.\n\n## The Multi-Scale Encoding: Why Different Dimensions Have Different Frequencies\n\nThe denominator $\\omega_i = 10000^{2i/d_{\\text{model}}}$ grows exponentially with $i$. At $i = 0$, $\\omega_0 = 1$ — the argument is just $\\text{pos}$, and the sine completes a full cycle every $2\\pi \\approx 6.28$ positions. At $i = d_{\\text{model}}/2 - 1$ (the last pair), $\\omega_{d/2-1} = 10000$ — the wavelength is $20000\\pi \\approx 62{,}832$ positions. That's one full cycle for every 62,832 tokens.\n\nThis is analogous to binary representation. In binary, the least significant bit flips every position, the next bit flips every two, the next every four, and so on. Sinusoidal encodings do the same thing continuously: dimension 0 oscillates fast (distinguishes adjacent tokens), dimension $d_{\\text{model}}-2$ oscillates so slowly it's essentially constant over any realistic sequence (but provides a coarse, long-range signal). The bit-pattern analogy was invoked in the original paper — each dimension is like a different bit, and the vector at each position is the encoding of that position in a continuous analog of binary.\n\nTogether, fine-grained and coarse-grained dimensions create a unique fingerprint at every scale simultaneously.\n\n![High-frequency dimensions (0–1) oscillate across every few positions while low-frequency dimensions (56–57) barely change across 100 positions](../Assets/blogs/positional-encodings-wavelengths.png)\n_The same formula, two very different behaviors. Left: dimension pair 0/1 (i=0, ω=1) completes a full cycle every ~6 positions — it cleanly separates \"trophy\" from \"was\" from \"big.\" Right: dimension pair 56/57 (i=28, ω≈5,623) changes by less than 0.02 across 100 positions — useless for distinguishing adjacent tokens, essential for distinguishing position 0 from position 50,000._\n\n## Worked Example: Encoding \"Trophy Was Big\" at $d_{\\text{model}} = 4$\n\nSticking with the same three tokens and 4-dimensional embeddings from the prior two posts. For $d_{\\text{model}} = 4$, there are two dimension pairs: $(i = 0)$ and $(i = 1)$.\n\n$$\\omega_0 = 10000^{0/4} = 1, \\qquad \\omega_1 = 10000^{2/4} = 100$$\n\nPosition encodings for pos = 0, 1, 2:\n\n**Step 1 — Compute PE for each position.**\n\n$$\\text{PE}(0) = [\\sin(0),\\; \\cos(0),\\; \\sin(0),\\; \\cos(0)] = [0,\\; 1,\\; 0,\\; 1]$$\n\n$$\\text{PE}(1) = [\\sin(1),\\; \\cos(1),\\; \\sin(0.01),\\; \\cos(0.01)] \\approx [0.841,\\; 0.540,\\; 0.010,\\; 1.000]$$\n\n$$\\text{PE}(2) = [\\sin(2),\\; \\cos(2),\\; \\sin(0.02),\\; \\cos(0.02)] \\approx [0.909,\\; -0.416,\\; 0.020,\\; 1.000]$$\n\n**Step 2 — Add to token embeddings.**\n\nThe token embeddings from the self-attention post:\n\n$$\\mathbf{x}_{\\text{trophy}} = [1, 0, 0, 1], \\quad \\mathbf{x}_{\\text{was}} = [0, 1, 0, 0], \\quad \\mathbf{x}_{\\text{big}} = [0, 0, 1, 1]$$\n\nAdding elementwise:\n\n$$\\tilde{\\mathbf{x}}_{\\text{trophy}} = [1+0,\\; 0+1,\\; 0+0,\\; 1+1] = [1.000,\\; 1.000,\\; 0.000,\\; 2.000]$$\n\n$$\\tilde{\\mathbf{x}}_{\\text{was}} = [0+0.841,\\; 1+0.540,\\; 0+0.010,\\; 0+1.000] = [0.841,\\; 1.540,\\; 0.010,\\; 1.000]$$\n\n$$\\tilde{\\mathbf{x}}_{\\text{big}} = [0+0.909,\\; 0+(-0.416),\\; 1+0.020,\\; 1+1.000] = [0.909,\\; -0.416,\\; 1.020,\\; 2.000]$$\n\n**Step 3 — Verify the relative-position property for k = 1, i = 0.**\n\nFor the rotation with offset $k = 1$ and $\\omega_0 = 1$:\n\n$$\\begin{bmatrix}\\text{PE}(1, 0) \\\\ \\text{PE}(1, 1)\\end{bmatrix} = \\begin{bmatrix}\\cos(1) & \\sin(1) \\\\ -\\sin(1) & \\cos(1)\\end{bmatrix} \\begin{bmatrix}\\text{PE}(0, 0) \\\\ \\text{PE}(0, 1)\\end{bmatrix} = \\begin{bmatrix}0.540 & 0.841 \\\\ -0.841 & 0.540\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}0 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix} = \\begin{bmatrix}0.841 \\\\ 0.540\\end{bmatrix}$$\n\nWhich matches $[\\sin(1), \\cos(1)] = [0.841, 0.540]$. The rotation matrix applied to position 0's encoding exactly recovers position 1's encoding. The same matrix applied to position 1 would recover position 2. The offset $k = 1$ is represented as a single fixed rotation — the model doesn't need to learn a different rule for each absolute position.\n\n**What these three vectors tell us.** Dims 0 and 1 differ substantially across all three positions — the high-frequency pair distinguishes \"trophy\" from \"was\" from \"big\" clearly. Dims 2 and 3 are nearly identical (0.010 vs 0.020, both ≈ 1.000) — the low-frequency pair contributes almost nothing at this scale, but would cleanly distinguish position 2 from position 2,000. The combined vector for each token is unique and carries position information at every scale.\n\nIn general: the position encoding for token $t$ is a $d_{\\text{model}}$-dimensional vector that acts as a unique, structured fingerprint for position $t$ — added directly to the semantic embedding before any attention is computed.\n\n## The General Formula\n\nLet $\\mathbf{X} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{n \\times d_{\\text{model}}}$ be the matrix of token embeddings (one row per token). Let $\\mathbf{PE} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{n \\times d_{\\text{model}}}$ be the positional encoding matrix. The input to the first Transformer layer is:\n\n$$\\tilde{\\mathbf{X}} = \\mathbf{X} + \\mathbf{PE}$$\n\nNo learned parameters in the encoding itself — $\\mathbf{PE}$ is computed deterministically from the formula and fixed. The model's $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ matrices then project $\\tilde{\\mathbf{X}}$ into query, key, and value spaces; positional information flows into attention patterns through those projections.\n\n## Learned vs. Sinusoidal: What the Data Shows\n\nThe natural question: why not learn a positional embedding — a lookup table of $n_{\\max}$ vectors, one per position, trained end-to-end? It's simpler, more flexible, and lets the model decide what position representation is actually useful for the task.\n\nVaswani et al. tested exactly this. From Table 3, row (E):\n\n| Encoding type      | PPL (dev) | BLEU (EN→DE dev) |\n| ------------------ | --------: | ---------------: |\n| Sinusoidal (base)  |      4.92 |             25.8 |\n| Learned embeddings |      4.92 |             25.7 |\n\nEssentially identical. The 0.1 BLEU difference is noise. On this task, the model doesn't care whether position comes from sinusoids or from learned vectors.\n\nThe reason to prefer sinusoidal isn't quality — it's generalization. A learned embedding table has entries for positions $0, 1, \\ldots, n_{\\max} - 1$. At inference on a sequence longer than $n_{\\max}$, there's nothing to look up. Sinusoidal encodings evaluate the formula at any integer, so a model trained on length-512 sequences can process a length-1024 sequence without modification — with some degradation, since the model hasn't seen those positions during training, but without a hard failure.\n\nThis matters more than it seems. Many production uses involve documents of variable and unpredictable length. Sinusoidal encodings give you a fallback. Learned embeddings give you an error.\n\nModern architectures have largely moved past both. Relative Position Encodings (Shaw et al. 2018), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE, Su et al. 2021), and ALiBi (Press et al. 2021) encode position directly into the attention score rather than adding it to the embedding — which allows better length generalization and avoids the \"position swamps semantics\" problem that can occur when adding PE and embedding vectors of similar magnitude. But those are extensions of the sinusoidal idea, not replacements for understanding it.\n\n## Code: Positional Encodings from Scratch\n\n```python\nimport numpy as np\n\ndef positional_encoding(n_positions, d_model):\n    \"\"\"\n    Compute the sinusoidal positional encoding matrix.\n\n    Args:\n        n_positions: number of positions to encode\n        d_model:     embedding dimension (must be even)\n\n    Returns:\n        PE: (n_positions, d_model) float array\n    \"\"\"\n    PE = np.zeros((n_positions, d_model))\n\n    for pos in range(n_positions):\n        for i in range(d_model // 2):\n            omega = 10000 ** (2 * i / d_model)   # wavelength scaling factor\n            PE[pos, 2*i]     = np.sin(pos / omega)\n            PE[pos, 2*i + 1] = np.cos(pos / omega)\n\n    return PE\n\n\ndef add_positional_encoding(X, d_model=None):\n    \"\"\"\n    Add positional encodings to a token embedding matrix.\n\n    Args:\n        X: (n, d_model) token embeddings\n        d_model: embedding dimension (inferred from X if not given)\n\n    Returns:\n        X_tilde: (n, d_model) embeddings with position injected\n    \"\"\"\n    n, d = X.shape\n    PE = positional_encoding(n, d)\n    return X + PE\n\n\n# ── Reproduce the worked example ──────────────────────────────────────────────\nX = np.array([\n    [1, 0, 0, 1],   # \"trophy\"\n    [0, 1, 0, 0],   # \"was\"\n    [0, 0, 1, 1],   # \"big\"\n], dtype=float)\n\nPE = positional_encoding(n_positions=3, d_model=4)\n\ntokens = [\"trophy\", \"was\", \"big\"]\nprint(\"Positional encodings (d_model=4):\")\nprint(f\"{'':>8}  {'dim0':>8}  {'dim1':>8}  {'dim2':>8}  {'dim3':>8}\")\nfor i, tok in enumerate(tokens):\n    vals = PE[i]\n    print(f\"{tok:>8}  {vals[0]:>8.3f}  {vals[1]:>8.3f}  {vals[2]:>8.3f}  {vals[3]:>8.3f}\")\n\nprint(\"\\nAfter adding to embeddings:\")\nX_tilde = add_positional_encoding(X)\nfor i, tok in enumerate(tokens):\n    vals = X_tilde[i]\n    print(f\"{tok:>8}  {vals[0]:>8.3f}  {vals[1]:>8.3f}  {vals[2]:>8.3f}  {vals[3]:>8.3f}\")\n\n# ── Verify the relative-position rotation property ─────────────────────────────\nprint(\"\\nVerifying PE(1) = R(k=1) @ PE(0) for dimension pair (0,1):\")\nk = 1\nomega_0 = 1.0\nR = np.array([\n    [ np.cos(k / omega_0), np.sin(k / omega_0)],\n    [-np.sin(k / omega_0), np.cos(k / omega_0)],\n])\npe0_pair = PE[0, :2]   # [sin(0), cos(0)] = [0, 1]\npredicted = R @ pe0_pair\nactual    = PE[1, :2]\nprint(f\"  R @ PE(0, dims 0-1) = {np.round(predicted, 3)}\")\nprint(f\"  PE(1, dims 0-1)     = {np.round(actual,    3)}\")\nprint(f\"  Match: {np.allclose(predicted, actual, atol=1e-10)}\")\n```\n\nThe final check confirms the rotation property: applying the $k=1$ rotation matrix to position 0's encoding exactly recovers position 1's encoding — numerically, to machine precision.\n\n## What Positional Encodings Still Cannot Do\n\n**They don't solve long-context degradation.** Sinusoidal encodings are well-defined at position 10,000, but the model was trained on sequences up to length 512. The attention patterns the model learned at position 3 were never paired with positional encodings from position 10,000. Applying the model to a 10,000-token sequence produces syntactically valid outputs, but their quality degrades significantly. This is the \"length generalization\" problem, and it's a real production constraint. RoPE and ALiBi were specifically designed to improve this.\n\n**They're added, not multiplied or gated.** The token embedding and the positional encoding are summed directly. For the sum to be meaningful, both components need to be in roughly the same numerical range. If the embedding weights initialize large and the positional encodings are bounded in $[-1, 1]$, position information is a small perturbation that the model can effectively ignore. In practice, initialization and layer normalization manage this, but it's a fragile balance — and one reason that learned encodings sometimes outperform sinusoidal ones on specific tasks where position is critical.\n\n**They encode position, not structure.** Position 5 is always position 5, regardless of whether the sentence is declarative or a question, whether it's inside a clause or at the top level. Hierarchical or syntactic structure isn't represented. Transformers deal with this implicitly through attention patterns, not through the positional encoding itself.\n\n**Absolute position isn't always what you want.** In translation, what matters is often relative position — \"this word is two positions ahead of that word\" — not whether the first token is at position 0 or position 47. The sinusoidal encoding provides both (through the rotation property), but extracting the relative signal still requires the model to compute the right attention pattern. Modern approaches like RoPE encode relative positions directly into the attention computation, which is more targeted and generally more effective.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Attention Is All You Need — Vaswani et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)\n- [Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations — Shaw et al. (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02155)\n- [RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding — Su et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864)\n- [Train Short, Test Long: ALiBi — Press et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409)\n";
